lines.text: Half a century of war, a hard-won freedom, and the world's newest country. This is the story of South Sudan.
From 1899 Britain and Egypt ruled Sudan together. In practice Britain governed, and it kept the south apart from the north.
In the south, on the White Nile, Juba grew from a small town. It would one day be a capital.
John Garang, born in 1945, would lead the southern rebels through their long war with the north.
Salva Kiir, born in 1951, would fight beside him, and later become the first president of a free south.
Even before Sudan's independence, the south rose against the north. The first civil war lasted from 1955 to 1972.
Manute Bol, born in 1962, would become one of the tallest players in NBA history, and give much of his money to his homeland.
In 1983 war came again. It lasted twenty-two years, one of the longest and deadliest of the century.
In 2005 a peace deal finally ended it, and promised the south a vote on its future. Months later, Garang died in a helicopter crash.
In January 2011 the people of the south voted, and almost all of them chose independence.
That July, the south broke away from Sudan, and crowds danced in the streets of Juba.
South Sudan was born, the newest widely recognised country in the world.
But only two years later, the president and his deputy fell out, and a new civil war raged until 2020.
Born from long struggle, South Sudan is still searching for lasting peace.
